title: Halakha, the path you walk
hookLine: halakha, Jewish law, heard as a path: decided by majority and precedent
carry: halakha is a path, walked step by step

lines: BUT WHAT DO I DO TODAY?
cards: Across a park there's a path nobody paved. No sign put it there. It's just where people walk, worn into the grass by one pair of shoes after another, until it's the obvious way across.

Newcomers follow it without thinking. It's not the only way through the park, but it's the way people take, and the more feet on it, the clearer it gets. Yesterday the Mishnah kept the minority's words.
But on an ordinary morning, a person has to know what to actually do. Today's word carries a path inside it.

teach.b: Halakha. It's the Hebrew name for Jewish law, the practical answer to how to live. First, what readers hear in it.
Tradition hears in the word the Hebrew verb for walking. In Exodus, Moses's father-in-law, Jethro, advises him to show the people, in the King James wording, "the way wherein they must walk."
So the law is pictured not as a wall of rules but as a path, walked step by step, every day. Second, how a path gets chosen.
The sages read a verse in Exodus about not following a crowd to do wrong, and drew from it a working rule: in a dispute among judges, go with the majority. Third, the majority isn't the whole story.

teach.h: THESE AND THESE; THE LAW FOLLOWS HILLEL.
teach.b: You met this verdict long ago, in tractate Eruvin: the schools of Hillel and Shammai argue for a long time, and a voice from heaven declares, these and these are the words of the living God, and the law follows the school of Hillel.
Both are words of the living God, but you can only walk one path at a time. And why Hillel?
The Talmud says they were gentle and humble, and taught the words of the school of Shammai too, even putting Shammai's words before their own. Fourth, precedent.
Once a path is walked, later teachers look at how earlier ones ruled and walk where they walked, the way a newcomer follows the worn path in the grass. Halakha isn't only a list.
It's a road with a lot of footprints already on it.

how: Jews who keep halakha look to it for how to live day to day, from food and prayer to business and family life, and often bring their questions to a rabbi, who weighs the majority view and earlier rulings.

games.q: two schools have argued for a long time. a heavenly voice says both are the words of the living God. you still need one ruling. which school's view becomes the law?
games.why: the law follows Hillel. the Talmud's reason: they were gentle and humble, and taught Shammai's words too, even before their own.

practice: If you can, stand and take a few slow steps across the room and back, feeling each foot land; if you'd rather stay seated, press your feet into the floor, one and then the other.
Either way, choose a direction before you move, and notice that choosing one doesn't make the others disappear. You're just going this way, now.

wordCard.voice: Halakha. Jewish law, heard as a path to walk, decided by the majority and carried forward by precedent. Today's word.
